title: boat vs GitHub Actions: agent machines, not 6-hour CI jobs
text:
GitHub Actions is GitHub's CI/CD service: workflows in your repository run as jobs on runners that GitHub hosts or that you host yourself.

GitHub Actions is a CI service, not a sandbox API. Each job on a GitHub-hosted runner gets a new VM, Linux and Windows on Azure and macOS on GitHub's own Mac fleet, with passwordless sudo, and the VM is gone when the job ends. It is built for building, testing and deploying the code in a repository, and GitHub's own Copilot cloud agent and the Claude and Codex agents on GitHub also run on Actions runners.

Kind of product

CI/CD service; jobs are defined in workflow files in a GitHub repository

Isolation

A new VM for each job; Linux and Windows on Azure, macOS on GitHub's own Mac cloud

Job length

Each job can run for up to 6 hours

Concurrency

20 jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise; macOS 5, or 50 on Enterprise

Allowed use

GitHub-hosted runners are for work on the repository's software project; reselling Actions as a service is not allowed

Self-hosted runners

Open-source runner under MIT; usage on self-hosted runners is free

title: CI with boat
text:
# CI with boat

> Run GitHub Actions jobs on boat sandboxes with runs-on: boat, or drive boat from any CI with the CLI.

Two ways to run CI on boat:

| Way | Setup | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub Actions runners | Install the boat CI GitHub App, change `runs-on` | Your CI is GitHub Actions |
| The CLI from any CI | An API key and a few `boat` commands | GitLab CI, CircleCI, Buildkite, or one step of a GitHub job |

## GitHub Actions runners: `runs-on: boat`

Each job gets a fresh sandbox, billed per second, deleted when the job ends.

CI needs the $20/month plan or higher. On the free trial, or without a plan, boat refuses each job once and says why in `boat ci` and on the dashboard. Start a plan, then re-run the job.

### Set up in 2 steps

1. Install the boat CI GitHub App on your GitHub organization or account. Pick the repositories:

```bash
boat ci connect            # jobs bill the wallet in scope (see `boat org`)
boat ci connect --org acme # jobs bill the acme organization

```

The command opens GitHub in your browser. GitHub asks you to authorize the app: boat uses that to check that you can manage the installation.

title: Celesto vs Boat CI: CI pricing and runners compared
text:
## Boat charges $0.018/hour, with a $20 monthly CI minimum.

Boat Small provides 2 vCPU and 4 GB for $0.018/hour. Celesto Standard costs $0.03/hour ($0.0005/min).

Boat CI requires a paid plan from $20/month. That payment becomes VM-time credit, so your base bill is the higher of the plan minimum and VM time.

The $20 plan includes 12 starts/minute, 60/hour, and 200/day. Starts beyond the allowances can add $0.03–$0.07 each. Many short jobs can make those charges larger than the VM-time bill.

Celesto charges computer runtime, including preparation and cleanup. There is no monthly runner plan or separate published start fee; workspace limits and available capacity still apply.

title: The Real Cost Math Behind Self-Hosted GitHub Actions Runners
text:
In December 2025, GitHub announced a new $0.002-per-minute platform charge that would apply to self-hosted runner usage starting March 2026. The backlash was immediate, and GitHub postponed the change within 48 hours “to re-evaluate our approach”. As of mid-2026, that fee has never taken effect, self-hosted runner usage remains free of any GitHub platform charge, and there’s no announced timeline for reintroducing it. A number of comparison sites and blog posts still describe the fee as active or upcoming. It isn’t, at least not right now.

What did actually happen on January 1, 2026 is the opposite of what you’d expect given the self-hosted fee scare: GitHub cut its own hosted-runner rates by up to 39%, folding a smaller platform charge into the hosted price rather than the self-hosted one. Current 2-core rates, listed on GitHub’s own Actions runner pricing reference, run $0.006 per minute for Linux, $0.010 for Windows, and $0.062 for macOS, all cheaper than they were in 2025.

...

Take a dedicated server with 24 physical cores, OpenMetal’s current Medium v4 tier, priced at $928.80 per month for the Ashburn configuration. If that server runs a mix of parallel CI jobs sized to match GitHub’s 2-core runner definition, it can host about 12 concurrent 2-core-equivalent job slots. To find the break-even point, divide the fixed monthly cost by the per-minute hosted rate: $928.80 ÷ $0.006 works out to roughly 154,800 minutes, or about 2,580 hours, of aggregate CI compute per month
